detail: Spanish-speaking countries split on this word. ALTO is Mexico and most of Central America; PARE is used across South America. Getting the word right narrows a whole continent to a region.
PARE covers most of South America in both Portuguese and Spanish. Once you see it, use road-line colour to split Brazil (yellow) from Argentina and Chile (white).

tell: Yellow diamond warning signs instead of red-bordered triangles.
detail: The world splits into diamond and triangle warning signs. Diamonds: the Americas, Ireland, Japan, Australia and New Zealand. Triangles: continental Europe, most of Africa and Asia. This is a one-glance hemisphere-level filter.
The Vienna Convention shape, used across Europe and much of Africa and Asia. Its presence rules out North America, Ireland, Japan and Australasia in a single look.

tell: Speed limits in a white circle with a thick red ring.
detail: Circular red-ringed speed limits are the European standard and are also used across most of Asia, Africa and South America. The number is in kilometres per hour.

tell: Rectangular black-on-white sign reading SPEED LIMIT above the number.
detail: The US spells it out on a plain white rectangle with no red ring, in miles per hour. Canada uses a rectangle too but writes MAXIMUM and uses km/h, which separates the two.

tell: Red-and-white chevron boards on the outside of bends.
detail: Chevron colour is a useful regional tag. Red and white dominates Europe; black on yellow is common in the Americas, Japan and parts of Asia; some countries use black on white.

tell: Black chevrons on a yellow board.
detail: Yellow chevron boards go with the yellow diamond warning-sign family. Seeing yellow chevrons alongside yellow centre lines is a strong North America pull.
